background.title: What a timed topic test is for
background.html:
A topic test checks one topic the way an exam does: a fixed time, no notes, marks printed in brackets after each question, for example [3]. Today the times come from the test covers: they are exam pace, a bit faster than normal homework.

The point is not the score. The point is to find out which exact points you cannot yet write down under time, so you can fix them before the exam.

background.title: How a mark scheme gives marks
background.html:
A mark scheme is the list of answers a marker accepts. For a written question it lists separate points, and each different correct point is worth one mark, up to the number in brackets. A scheme often lists more points than there are marks ("any 4 of these details").

  • Say the same thing twice: still one mark.
  • Your words can differ from the scheme if the meaning is the same.
  • For a calculation, the working is part of the marks.

background.title: Command words: what the question wants
background.html:
The first word of a question tells you how much to write.

  • List or state: short answers, no explanation.
  • Outline: the main points, briefly.
  • Describe: say what something is like or what happens.
  • Explain: say why or how, with "because" and "so".
  • Distinguish: make the differences clear.
  • Suggest: a sensible idea, even for something you were not taught.

background.title: Rate: how fast something happens
background.html:
A rate is a change divided by the time it took. If 0.55 units of glucose appear in 5 minutes, the rate is 0.55 ÷ 5 = 0.11 units per minute.

On a graph, a steep line is a fast rate, a flat line means nothing is happening any more. Always write "per minute" (min−1) in the unit of a rate.

terms.def: The list of answers the marker accepts, with how many marks each point earns.
Done against a clock, with the time limit of the real exam, and no notes.
Higher level: the longer Biology course you take. HL exams have extra questions on the HL-only parts.
Standard level: the shorter Biology course. The tests show the SL time and total too, but you use the HL ones.
A question with answers A, B, C and D where you pick one. One mark each.
A question split into short parts, each worth a few marks.
A longer written answer, worth about 4 to 8 marks, where you make several separate points.
Writing down everything you remember about a topic on a blank page, from memory, before you look at anything.
Short revision notes for each topic (Revision Village, in your Drive), one or two pages long.
A protein that speeds up one particular chemical reaction in a living thing without being used up.
The pocket on an enzyme where the substrate fits and the reaction happens.
The molecule an enzyme works on. Sucrose is the substrate of invertase.
An enzyme that splits sucrose (table sugar) into glucose and fructose.
Splits a molecule into smaller ones by adding water.
A single sugar unit, such as glucose or fructose.
A substance that slows down or stops an enzyme.
The bacterial enzyme that builds cross-links in the bacterial cell wall. Penicillin blocks it.
An inhibitor binds in the active site and becomes fixed there for good, so that enzyme molecule can never work again. Penicillin is the example.
Cannot be undone.
A random change in the base sequence of DNA. It can change the shape of a protein.
Binding at a second site on an enzyme, away from the active site, which changes the shape of the active site.
The first stage of cell respiration, in the cytoplasm: glucose is split into two pyruvate, making a little ATP.
Adenosine triphosphate: the small molecule that carries energy to wherever the cell needs it.
Cell respiration: the chemical reactions in cells that release energy from food molecules to make ATP. Not the same as breathing.
Apparatus that measures how fast living things use oxygen, from the change in gas volume in a sealed tube.
A chemical that absorbs carbon dioxide, so only the oxygen used changes the gas volume.
When a seed starts to grow.
In an experiment, a set-up that leaves out the thing being tested (here, glass beads instead of beans) to show the result is caused by it.
Anything in an experiment that can change, such as temperature. You change one and keep the others the same.
Using oxygen. Aerobic respiration releases much more energy than anaerobic respiration (without oxygen).
The jelly-like inside of a cell, outside the nucleus, where many reactions happen.
Small parts inside a cell (one is a mitochondrion) where aerobic respiration makes most of the ATP.
A helper molecule that picks up hydrogen in respiration (becoming reduced NAD) and hands it on to the electron transport chain.
A chain of proteins in the mitochondrion that passes on electrons from hydrogen and uses their energy to make most of the ATP.
An enzyme that removes hydrogen from a molecule.
Many more protons (hydrogen ions, H<sup>+</sup>) on one side of a membrane than the other. Their flow back drives ATP making.
Making ATP using the flow of protons back across a membrane through the enzyme ATP synthase.
The -NH<sub>2</sub> group at one end of an amino acid.
The -COOH group at the other end of an amino acid.
The central carbon atom of an amino acid, holding the amine group, the carboxyl group, a hydrogen and the R group.
The part of an amino acid that is different in each of the 20 kinds.
The bond joining two amino acids, made in a condensation reaction (water is given off).
Amino acids your body cannot make, so they must come from food.
Folded into a rounded shape; usually soluble. Enzymes and insulin are globular.
Long and thread-like; usually insoluble and strong. Collagen is fibrous.
A protein with a non-protein part attached, such as the haem group in haemoglobin.
The overall 3D folded shape of one protein chain.
IB command word: give the main points briefly.
IB command word: say why or how, with reasons (use "because" and "so").
